newsitem.title: USA: Reynolds document draws cancer link - expert.
newsitem.headline: Reynolds document draws cancer link - expert.

text.p: An internal R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co document told company executives 44 years ago that cigarette smoking caused cancer, an expert witness said Tuesday at the trial of a wrongful death lawsuit against Reynolds.

The document, written by Reynolds' researcher Claude Teague and dated February 1953, summarized statistical studies of the day and noted concurrent increases in cigarette smoking and lung cancer in the first half of the century.

It was introduced on the fourth day of testimony by Dr. Allan Feingold, a Miami physician called as an expert witness by lawyers for plaintiff Dana Raulerson, who sued R.J. Reynolds on behalf of the estate of her sister Jean Connor, a heavy smoker who died in October 1995 at age 49.
Asked if the tobacco company knew as a result of the document that cigarette smoking caused cancer, Feingold said: "They definitely knew."

The paper, titled "Survey of Cancer Research with Emphasis Upon Possible Carcinogens from Tobacco," compiled research available before 1953, including statistical surveys. It said scientists had found a rise in lung cancer in the 20th century and noted a link between a rise in cigarette smoking and the high incidence of lung cancer.

"The closely parallel increase in cigarette smoking has led to the suspicion that tobacco smoking is an important etiologic factor in the induction of primary cancer of the lung," the document concluded.

"Studies of clinical data tend to confirm the relationship between heavy and prolonged tobacco smoking and incidence of cancer of the lung," it said. "Extensive though inconclusive testing of tobacco substances on animals indicates the probable presence of carcinogenic agents in those substances."

The document further recommended that all tobacco additives, including "flavorants and humectants used by this company" should be carefully examined "with respect to their possible role as carcinogens or carcinogen-producing agents."

Lawyers for Raulerson have argued that executives at R.J. Reynolds, a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp, knew tobacco was addictive and caused cancer but failed to do anything about it. Connor began smoking in her teens and eventually developed a three-pack-a-day habit.
Feingold was due back on the witness stand Tuesday afternoon and had yet to be cross-examined by Reynolds' lawyers.
